WHY WE’RE BUILDING REZ1

Delegating the task
is only the beginning.

The real work is keeping context, execution, and review connected.

Coding agents can move quickly. Developers still need to understand what changed, what ran, and whether the result meets the original task. Switching between a chat, a terminal, and a diff makes that harder.

We’re designing rez1 around one complete loop: give an agent a bounded task, follow its work, and make an informed decision about the changes.

THE FIRST RELEASE

One task. Four deliberate steps.

Our initial milestone is a local repository-to-diff workflow.
Each step keeps the next decision visible.

01

Bring your repository

Start with an existing local Git repository. Create a separate worktree for the task so the main checkout stays intact.

Repository + task branch
02

Define the outcome

Describe the change, its scope, and how to validate it. Begin with one agent integration and a focused objective.

Context + acceptance criteria
03

Follow the work

See the files read, edits proposed, and checks requested. Approve commands before execution and keep actual results visible.

Activity + command approvals
04

Review the diff

Compare the proposed changes with the task and its test results. Decide what to keep before merging or pushing.

Changes + human review

OUR PLANNED CLAUDE INTEGRATION

Reason about the code.
Keep people in the loop.

We’re developing rez1 workspace, an open-source coding-agent workspace for local and cloud developer workflows. Our first milestone is a local repository-to-diff workflow, with a planned Claude integration for coding tasks and human review of proposed changes.

The integration design connects Claude to a bounded set of repository tools. The local coordinator would handle tool approvals, execution, and the review state.

Read the integration design
Integration planIN DESIGN
  1. 01

    Understand the task

    Provide the objective and relevant repository context.

  2. 02

    Request tools deliberately

    Read files and propose edits within the task workspace.

  3. 03

    Validate with approval

    Ask to run checks and record their actual outcomes.

  4. 04

    Return a reviewable result

    Present the diff, checks, and unresolved questions.

The Claude adapter is planned. No integration or partnership is claimed.

THE PROJECT BEHIND THE WORKSPACE

Independent.
Open source.
Built with intention.

rez1 started with a simple question: what should the workspace around a coding agent look like?

The project began in November 2025. The website and public repository launched in October 2026.

We’re beginning with the foundation rather than promising every workflow at once. The goal is a small, understandable system that helps developers move from a task to a change they can confidently review.

A FEW GOOD QUESTIONS

Before you dive in.

What exists now, what comes next,
and how to get involved.

Can I run a coding agent in rez1 today?

The current release is the project foundation: this website, the public repository, and design documentation. The local agent runtime is the next milestone. The interactive example on this page is an illustration, not a live agent.

What will the first version do?

Open an existing local Git repository, create an isolated task worktree, run one agent integration with visible activity and command approvals, and present the resulting diff and checks for human review.

How will rez1 use Claude?

We plan to use Claude for repository exploration and coding tasks through a tool-enabled adapter. The local coordinator will manage tool permissions, command execution, cancellation, and review. This integration is not implemented yet.

Will it work locally and in the cloud?

The first runtime is local. Cloud execution is a later phase that needs isolated environments, per-task credentials, quotas, and cleanup. The goal is to keep the same task and review experience in both environments.

Is the project open source?

Yes. The current website and project documentation are available under the MIT license in the public repository. Model services and third-party dependencies have their own terms.

How can I help?

Read the MVP specification, open an issue with a developer workflow you want to improve, or contact the maintainer. Focused feedback and small contributions are welcome while the local workflow takes shape.
